talks.title: The Phantom Circuit: the Lazarus Group's evolution in supply chain compromise
talks.teaser: Details the Phantom Circuit: the Lazarus Groups evolution in supply chain compromise and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview: Ryan Shabbidoff of SecurityScorecard presents at Virus Bulletin on the Phantom Circuit campaign—Lazarus Group's evolution in supply chain compromise through fake recruitment schemes.

Key Topics: DPRK IT worker infiltration schemes; fake recruiter personas targeting developers; cryptocurrency wallet compromise objectives; tracing obfuscated networks to Pyongyang; and India's tech sector targeting in 2025.

Technical Details: Shabbidoff traces the campaign from broad infections to precision sector targeting, adding 233 new victims by January 2025 with 110+ in India's technology sector. Research maps infrastructure to operator IPs in North Korea.

Takeaways: Lazarus Group exploits developer trust through elaborate recruitment fraud. Organizations must vet remote hiring pipelines and monitor for anomalous developer access patterns.

talks.title: Collaborative response to emerging critical RCE vulnerabilities in exposed edge devices
talks.teaser: Provides collaborative response to emerging critical RCE vulnerabilities in exposed edge devices and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Shadowserver Mission

The Shadowserver Foundation CEO describes the nonprofit's role responding to critical RCE vulnerabilities in exposed edge devices. With roughly 30 staff, they collaborate globally rather than operating as a commercial vendor.

Free Threat Intelligence Model

Shadowserver provides no-cost, network-scoped threat data to defenders worldwide—governments, ISPs, and organizations receive intelligence only about their own assets, raising the global security baseline. They monitor exposed endpoints continuously for internet-wide early warning.

Collaborative Response

When edge-device vulnerabilities emerge, Shadowserver works with national CERTs, law enforcement, researchers, and community partners to identify vulnerable devices, detect exploitation, reverse implants or webshells, and broadcast findings to incident responders.

Sustainability and Reach

Operating costs roughly $5 million annually, funded primarily by government grants and philanthropy, the organization serves defenders across 175 countries and territories while maintaining technical fingerprinting and disruption capabilities.

talks.title: European PDNS Readiness
talks.teaser: Details european PDNS Readiness and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
DNS4EU and Sovereignty

George Bhai outlines the EU-funded DNS4EU project to keep protective DNS processing inside Europe, addressing NIS2 concerns that commercial filtering often sends citizen DNS data abroad. William’s half of the talk covers threat feeds and intelligence processing.

Government Adoption Challenges

National CERT maturity varies widely: some agencies are independent with budgets, while others depend on parliament to fund projects. Deployments range from cloud resolver-only protection for schools to full national hierarchies with on-prem resolvers for ministries and hospitals.

Multi-Tenant Architecture

DNS for Gov proposes vertical tenants so ministries do not share blocklists or telemetry. Per-organization domain grading lets hospitals block adult content while police investigative units retain broader access, with auditing options for compliance.

Scale of the Problem

Europe has billions of connected devices and high DNS abuse rates. The speakers argue four in five devices face malicious campaigns, motivating centralized protective DNS as a public-sector readiness initiative.

talks.title: Arachnid alert: Latrodectus loader crawls through defences
talks.teaser: Presents arachnid alert: Latrodectus loader crawls through defences and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Malware overview

VMRay's Albert introduces Latrodectus, first seen October 2023, as a loader/downloader with partial backdoor behavior, DLL payloads with four exports to one address, and links to TA577/TA578 and IcedID/Pikabot infrastructure.

Version evolution

Encryption moved from XOR with PRNG to rolling XOR/incrementer, then AES-CTR in v1.4+, with ongoing C2 command changes into 2025 v2.x.

Delivery

Early DocuSign-themed phishing led victims through obfuscated JavaScript to MSI installers bundling the DLL via custom actions. Recent campaigns injected sites with Cloudflare-themed clickfix overlays and Telegram-bot-driven JavaScript retrieval.

Evasion and analysis

Checks include process counts by Windows version, MAC address length, PEB BeingDebugged, and 32-on-64 process detection; anti-analysis uses runtime API resolution, CRC32 hashing, and evolving string encryption. Network beacons include a volume-serial-derived GUID and FNV1a-hashed campaign group IDs useful for detection.

talks.title: Smashing smishing by quashing quishing
talks.teaser: Presents smashing smishing by quashing quishing and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Andrew Brandt, principal researcher at Netcraft and former cybercrime journalist, traces how QR-code phishing ("quishing") evolved from targeted smishing into a widespread 2025 threat.

## Attack Mechanics
Victims receive messages with QR codes whose URLs often embed the target's email address. Domains are frequently registered one day before attacks. Landing pages frame legitimate Microsoft login flows inside weaponized pages whose scripts capture credentials and MFA codes in real time.

## Phishing Kits and Scale
Brandt links campaigns to kits such as Onyx, Tycoon 2FA, and Rockstar 2FA that proxy authentic login pages. He highlights a mobile UX problem: photographing a QR code on screen often triggers the link accidentally. At Netcraft, similar quishing lures now appear across many industries.

## Takeaways
Defenders should treat quishing like credential phishing, monitor freshly registered domains, and train users that QR codes are untrusted hyperlinks—not harmless images.
